articles.title: Your iPhone may die faster this week: Here’s why
articles.summary: As annoying as it may be, it should be short-lived.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — The latest major update from Apple, iOS 27, was released to qualifying devices on Monday, bringing with it a slew of improvements and new features to iPhones, iPads, and more.

This marks the second major iOS update in Apple’s new naming system. Last year, Apple broke from the numerical pattern it had been following, naming the annual update iOS 26 rather than the expected iOS 19.

But, like all system updates before it, iOS 27 is massive, requiring several gigabytes of space on your iPhone or other Apple devices. A lack of space may be one of a handful of obstacles standing between you and the newest Apple features.

Once you are able to download iOS 27 on your iPhone or iPad, you may notice yourself reaching for the charger more frequently than you were last week.

Apple has previously warned that major iOS updates can temporarily have a negative impact on your device’s battery life.

“Immediately after completing an update, particularly a major release, you might notice a temporary impact on battery life and thermal performance,” the company says on a support page . “This is normal, as your device needs time to complete the setup process in the background, including indexing data and files for search, downloading new assets, and updating apps.”

It typically lasts for only a few days while your device continues behind-the-scenes work. However, Apple also warns that your use of your iPhone or iPad will continue to have an impact on the battery. If you’re exploring the new features from iOS 27, you may be a contributing factor in your device dying more quickly.

It is also recommended that you do not allow your iPhone to charge to 100% during these draining times. Experts and phone manufacturers generally advise charging only to 80% to prolong the battery life.

articles.title: Scammers know the best time to text you
articles.summary: Malwarebytes data reveals scam texts peak around noon ET with 874% higher volume than overnight, and Fridays bring roughly 50% more messages.
articles.body: If your phone seems to light up with suspicious texts right when your day gets busy, you may not be imagining it. New research from cybersecurity company Malwarebytes suggests scammers have gotten much more strategic about when they contact you and where they do it. The company analyzed global threat data collected between April 15 and July 14, 2026. Researchers tracked more than 20 scam categories. They found that criminals often choose the platform that gives a particular scam the best chance of working. Then there is the timing. For Americans, scam text volume peaked around 12 p.m. ET. That was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET, the quietest hour Malwarebytes observed. Scam text volume also climbed as the week went on. It reached its highest point on Friday, when people received roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week. That tells me scammers are paying attention to more than what they send you. They are also watching when you may be most likely to see it. And the timing is only part of the strategy, because the type of scam often determines exactly where they try to reach you. THE SCAM TEXT TEST: SPOT DANGER BEFORE YOU TAP NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Scammers are choosing the best place to reach you Different scams tend to favor different platforms. Malwarebytes found that job scams commonly arrive through email. Romance scams favor social media, where conversations with new people feel more natural. Meanwhile, tech support scams frequently start with a phone call. That makes sense when you think about how each scam works. A fake recruiter can blend into a busy inbox. Someone starting a conversation on social media may seem harmless. A caller claiming your computer has a serious problem can immediately put you under pressure. The channel becomes part of the trick. We've seen that with changing tech support scams. They can now begin with fake invoices, bogus security alerts or convincing support pages. The web remains scammers' favorite doorway You hear plenty about scam texts and suspicious DMs. However, the web remains the leading way scams reach people in Malwarebytes' data. Email came next, followed by SMS. Malwarebytes says it blocks around 500,000 phishing websites every day. That number gives you an idea of how many fake pages criminals keep pushing online. Some copy banks or popular retailers. Others imitate technology companies or government services. A link in a text can take you straight to one of these pages. The fake site may look polished enough to fool you at first glance. So, when a message says something has gone wrong with an account, resist the urge to use the link it provides. Open the company's app yourself or type the website address directly into your browser. Scam texts hit their peak around lunchtime Here's the part that really caught my attention. Malwarebytes found that scam texts targeting Americans reached their highest volume around 12 p.m. ET. At noon, volume was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET. Think about what your phone habits look like around lunchtime. You could be leaving a meeting, grabbing something to eat or checking messages between errands. Your attention may already be split. Then a text arrives saying your package cannot be delivered. Another claims you owe a toll. Maybe a message warns that somebody accessed your account. That timing can work in a scammer's favor because you may react before giving the message a closer look. Of course, a text arriving at noon does not automatically mean somebody is trying to scam you. The data shows when Malwarebytes observed the highest volume. Still, the pattern gives us another look at how organized scam campaigns have become. IS THAT TRAFFIC TICKET TEXT A SCAM OR REAL? Fridays bring even more scam texts The day of the week also appears to play a role. Malwarebytes saw its lowest scam text volume on Sunday. Activity then increased as the week went on. By Friday, people were receiving roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week. The researchers cannot say exactly why Friday produced the highest volume. However, the pattern suggests scammers may be deliberately timing campaigns instead of sending messages at random. Maybe you're finishing work and thinking about the weekend. You could also be juggling deliveries, travel plans or bills. Whatever the reason, criminals want you moving quickly. That's something we've seen repeatedly with fake government messages. A DMV scam text can threaten fines or license problems while pushing you toward a payment page. The threat gets your attention. The deadline tries to stop you from thinking. MrBeast is the most impersonated person in the data Timing gets the message in front of you. Familiarity can make you trust it. Malwarebytes found that Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, was the most impersonated person in its data. His likeness appeared in about 30% of impersonation scams observed by the company. Elon Musk and Donald Trump followed him in the data. These scams can involve fake cryptocurrency giveaways or schemes that demand a fee before you supposedly receive money. The real person has nothing to do with the offer. Scammers borrow a face you recognize because familiarity can lower your guard. That tactic has become even more troubling as AI-generated video and cloned voices improve. A face on your screen no longer proves the person actually made the video. Google leads the list of impersonated brands Scammers use the same strategy with companies you recognize. According to reports from Malwarebytes users, the five most impersonated brands were: Google, Microsoft, Apple, Roblox and Amazon. Google's name appeared at least twice as often as Amazon's. That familiarity gives criminals a huge advantage. If you use Google every day, a fake security warning may look routine. An Apple customer may react quickly to a message about an account problem. Amazon scams can land at exactly the right moment because so many of us regularly have packages on the way. So, treat the logo as decoration until you verify the message yourself. Gaming scams are getting more attention Gaming communities are also attracting scammers. Malwarebytes found Roblox, Steam, Discord and Minecraft among the most impersonated gaming platforms. Roblox scam activity increased 15% between mid-June and mid-July. Steam saw a 19% increase during the same period. The potential losses can also get serious. Malwarebytes says about half of the gaming scams it analyzed could lead to losses of $1,000 or more. That is particularly concerning when younger gamers may encounter fake offers through communities they already trust. A message promising free in-game items or access to something exclusive can quickly lead to a fake login page. Once the victim enters a password, the scammer may take over the account. AMAZON JOB SCAM TEXTS ARE SPREADING AGAIN WITH A NEW TWIST How to protect yourself from better-timed scams Scammers can improve their timing, but you can make yourself a much harder target. The best defense starts with slowing down and verifying what you see. 1) Don't click links or call numbers in unexpected messages Avoid links and phone numbers inside unsolicited emails, texts or social media messages. A link can take you to a copied website designed to steal your login or payment information. Likewise, the phone number in a fake security alert can connect you directly to the scammer. Instead, leave the message and contact the company another way. 2) Verify the message through an official source Go directly to the company's official website or open its app. If the message claims you owe money, check your real account before paying anything. You can also contact the organization using a phone number you already trust. This breaks the scammer's control over the conversation. 3) Be careful with sponsored search results Searching for a company's website can help, but pay close attention to what you click. Scammers can use sponsored search ads that lead to fake support pages or convincing copies of legitimate websites. Check the web address before entering sensitive information. When possible, use a saved bookmark or the company's official app. 4) Keep passwords and verification codes private Never give someone your password because they called or messaged you unexpectedly. The same goes for PINs, account recovery codes and one-time verification codes. A scammer may claim they need a code to verify your identity. In reality, that code may give them access to your account. If a caller asks for sensitive information, hang up and contact the organization yourself. 5) Never send payment because someone pressures you Be suspicious when an unexpected caller or message demands immediate payment. Before paying, confirm the charge through your actual account or by contacting the organization independently. Watch closely for payment requests involving gift cards, cryptocurrency or transfers that may be difficult to reverse. Urgency should make you more cautious, not less. 6) Use browser protection against scam sites Strong antivirus software can help block known phishing sites and other malicious pages. Browser protection can also warn you before you enter information on a dangerous website. Keep your browser updated as well. Security updates help close weaknesses that criminals may try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 7) Turn on scam and spam filtering on your phone Your phone may already include tools that identify suspicious calls or messages. Turn on spam filtering when your device and messaging app support it. Mobile security software can provide another layer of protection by identifying scam texts and dangerous links. No filter catches everything, so continue checking unexpected messages yourself. 8) Check suspicious messages before responding If something feels wrong, look into it before you reply. Search for the company's official contact information. Check your account directly. You can also use a reputable scam-checking service to examine a suspicious phone number, message or link. The goal is simple. Verify the claim somewhere outside the conversation the scammer started. 9) Block and report scam messages Once you know a message is fraudulent, block the sender and report it as spam. Most phones and email services include built-in reporting options. Reporting scams can also help providers identify campaigns and block similar messages for other users. Then delete the message so you do not accidentally interact with it later. Act quickly if you already clicked or shared information If you entered a password on a suspicious site, change it immediately using the real website or app. Change that password anywhere else you reused it. Better yet, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account so one stolen password cannot unlock several accounts. If you gave away payment information, contact your bank or card issuer right away. You should also review your accounts for unfamiliar activity. If a scammer gained access to your device, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan. Kurt's key takeaways What grabs me about this research is how deliberate scam campaigns are becoming. Scammers are paying attention to where you spend your time. Now, the timing data suggests they may also be watching when you're more likely to respond. That changes how I think about those random-looking texts that pop up during a busy day. The message may feel like one more thing that needs your attention. That's exactly when you need to slow down. You cannot control when a scammer contacts you. You can control whether that person gets to set the pace. When something unexpected asks for money or account information, get out of the message. Find the real company on your own and check the claim there. That small pause can ruin a scammer's entire plan. Have you noticed more scam texts arriving around lunchtime or toward the end of the week, and what kind of message almost fooled you into responding? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Ranked: Which Countries Rely Most on U.S. Trade
articles.summary: The United States absorbs just 18% of exports for the average G20 country. For Canada and Mexico, there's a lot more dependence.
articles.body:
Which G20 Countries Rely Most on the U.S. for Exports?

The U.S. absorbs 18% of the average G20 economy's exports.

Canada and Mexico each ship roughly three-quarters of their goods exports to the U.S.

Just 0.9% of Russia's exports go to the U.S., the lowest share among G20 countries.

Access to the United States, the world's largest economy, remains crucial for countries around the world. However, America's closest neighbors rely far more heavily on the U.S. market than other major global economies.

This visualization ranks Group of 20 (G20) countries by the share of their goods exports sent to the U.S., using the latest available data (2025) from UN Comtrade and the Observatory for Economic Complexity .

Only goods trade is included. The African Union and European Union are excluded despite being G20 members.

Canada and Mexico are particularly exposed to shifts in U.S. trade policy because of their deeply integrated trade relationships with the United States.

The U.S. absorbs 72.3% of Canadian exports and 81.9% of Mexican exports, compared with just 18.1% for the average G20 economy. This makes both countries particularly vulnerable to changes in U.S. trade policy.

The table below lists G20 economies alongside the U.S. share of their exports in 2025.

Decades of economic integration have helped produce this concentration. The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which entered into force in 1994, reduced trade barriers between Canada, Mexico, and the United States. It was replaced by the USMCA in 2020.

More recently, the second Trump administration has imposed tariffs on both U.S. neighbors. Talks between Ottawa and Washington have broken down, leading to the imposition of retaliatory tariffs .

Meanwhile, Mexico, the most exposed G20 country, continues negotiations with the U.S. in an effort to avoid further tariffs on its agricultural and automotive sectors.

Outside North America, no G20 country sends a comparable share of its exports to the United States. However, traditional U.S. allies including Japan (18.6%), South Korea (17.4%), and the United Kingdom (15.9%) still send substantial portions of their goods exports to the U.S.

articles.title: Carney Says US Deal Possible, Blow-Up Helped Clarify ‘Red Lines’
articles.summary: The dramatic collapse of trade talks with the US in August helped clarify Canada’s negotiating “red lines,” said Prime Minister Mark Carney, who added he’s r...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The dramatic collapse of trade talks with the US in August helped clarify Canada's negotiating "red lines," said Prime Minister Mark Carney, who added he's ready to get back to the table for the right deal.

In an interview with Bloomberg News, he was asked whether it's a question of who moves first to get negotiations restarted.

"There's not a pride thing from our perspective," he said. "We're practical people that know what our bottom lines are, what our red lines are for sovereignty, for culture, not being restricted on our ability to sign other trade deals."

The prime minister added: "I think our American colleagues maybe, perhaps, understand those red lines a little more clearly now, given what's happened. We're ready to sit down."

But Canada is "not going to slow down" on its efforts to expand trade with other countries, said Carney, who has invited the world's leading money managers to Toronto this week for the inaugural Canada Investment Summit — a bid to pull in more foreign direct investment. As soon as it ends, he'll fly to France for talks on deepening Canada's relationship with the European Union.

Top-level discussions between the US and Canada fell apart on Aug. 21 over a deal that would have reduced US tariffs on core Canadian sectors like steel and automotive, while eliminating a number of Canadian trade restrictions.

The next day, President Donald Trump's administration implemented 50% tariffs against about $20 billion of Canadian exports. Canada has retaliated with counter-tariffs hitting the same total dollar value of US exports.

Both sides blamed each other for the blow-up and claimed each had made last-minute demands. Carney said the US wanted to infringe on Canadian cultural protections around the French language and restrict Canada's ability to sign other trade deals.

Despite this, on Saturday, Trump said a deal with Canada could come "fairly soon," without elaborating.

Carney said he welcomed those comments and added Canada's ready to sit down for a deal that respects each side's sovereignty and Canada's cultural institutions.

"We'll sit down when it makes sense. Canada and the US have a very long relationship. We sometimes go through periods where there are tensions in that relationship. Provided we continue this approach, we'll come to some some agreement at some point."

articles.title: Ballmer apologizes as Clippers accept $30M salary cap circumvention fine
articles.summary: Billionaire owner Steve Ballmer has apologized for his role in an effort by the Los Angeles Clippers to circumvent the NBA’s salary cap by funneling money to star player Kawhi Leonard through endorsement opportunities. “This has been a very difficult time for everybody associated with the Clippers, and for that, I have sincere regrets,” Ballmer…
articles.body:
Billionaire owner Steve Ballmer has apologized for his role in an effort by the Los Angeles Clippers to circumvent the NBA’s salary cap by funneling money to star player Kawhi Leonard through endorsement opportunities.

“This has been a very difficult time for everybody associated with the Clippers, and for that, I have sincere regrets,” Ballmer said in a statement issued late Sunday night. “I want to apologize to our fans, employees, and my fellow NBA team owners for the distraction and distress this matter has caused, for which I accept responsibility as principal owner.”

The Clippers were docked five draft picks and fined $30 million earlier this month, and Ballmer was banned for a year from basketball activities as punishment for the scheme.

The club initially pushed back on the NBA’s punishment, among the steepest handed down to a team in the league’s history, calling it “the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence.”

Ballmer took a softer tone in his Sunday statement.

“We are committing to put this chapter behind us. We have communicated to the NBA that we are complying with the penalties assessed by the league, have paid the fine, and are moving forward,” the former Microsoft executive and one of the NBA’s richest owners said. “While there are still disagreements concerning the findings in the report, this is not where I want to focus. Team owners should support, not distract.”

The Clippers owner’s apology comes amid reports President Trump’s Department of Justice is investigating the club in connection with the Leonard scandal, though it is unclear whether Ballmer or Leonard are the subject of the criminal probe.

articles.title: AI leaders call for development slowdown
articles.summary: A growing chorus of artificial intelligence leaders are calling for a slowdown of the technology’s development following a researcher’s ominous warning that AI could soon destroy humanity. Shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called to slow down AI capability development, several of his competitors, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk, followed…
articles.body:
A growing chorus of artificial intelligence leaders are calling for a slowdown of the technology’s development following a researcher’s ominous warning that AI could soon destroy humanity.

Shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called to slow down AI capability development , several of his competitors, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk, followed suit.

The calls followed a post from 27-year-old AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who claimed researchers at the firms “believe AI could kill all humans” but still push forward in a race to develop superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance. Coxon resigned from Anthropic before sharing his warnings on social media.

In a lengthy post on X , Altman said the “world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened.”

“Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot,” Altman said.

Altman reiterated OpenAI’s support of a federal framework for safety requirements, but also argued the industry does not need to wait for legislation or an antitrust exemption to create “consistent rules” and shared values along the firms.

Altman said pacing development does not mean stopping, but that development “should be slower than it otherwise could be.”

“Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring,” Altman said.

Musk, who originally co-founded OpenAI with Altman, reposted Amodei as well, writing that “Dario is right.”

The comments mark a shift for AI leaders, who have shied away from any commitments to slow down until recently.

Researchers have warned of AI’s potential danger for years, but nothing struck a chord quite like Coxon’s social media thread.

Coxon’s assessment went viral with more than 165 million views and within a few hours, the debate over the long-term implications of artificial intelligence was no longer confined within the technology community.

Coxon is among a camp of what critics dubbed AI “doomers,” who believe the technology will lead to mass extinction if development is not safety-aligned or slowed down.

“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” Coxon wrote on social media. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, affirmed Coxon’s warning, stating, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans !”

articles.title: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree to avoid energy targets as fuel prices rise
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to avoid energy targets in their ongoing war as global fuel prices rise. “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The post comes as both gasoline and diesel prices are rising worldwide.…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to avoid energy targets in their ongoing war as global fuel prices rise.

“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

The post comes as both gasoline and diesel prices are rising worldwide. Refining capacity shortages are a factor in the high prices, as global conflicts take out refineries.

U.S. diesel prices recently crossed $6 per gallon for the first time ever and averaged $6.23 per gallon on Monday, according to AAA. Gasoline prices averaged about $4.32 per gallon.

The high prices have created issues for the White House going into the midterms. Trump, in his post, sought to distance his administration and its decision to go to war with Iran from the issue.

“The World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran,” he said.

In a social media post of his own , Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his nation “is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement.”

“If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes,” Zelensky wrote, adding, “We expect specifics from our partners.”

Experts have said that the Russia-Ukraine conflict is playing a part, but it’s not the only thing driving up prices, as Middle East instability is also factor.

“Average gasoline and diesel prices rose in every state over the last week as geopolitical tensions escalated on multiple fronts, with friction between the U.S. and Iran, new hostilities in the Red Sea, and the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline all combining to jolt prices sharply higher,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy in a statement posted online . “New weekend attacks also knocked two additional Russian refineries offline, further straining global refined product supplies and likely offsetting any seasonal relief.”

Laura Kelly contributed. Updated at 12:38 p.m. EDT

articles.title: States and cities sue over ‘public charge’ green card restrictions
articles.summary: A coalition of Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration to block a rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards or even enter the country if they rely on public benefits. The 22 states and D.C. are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) “public charge” rule, set…
articles.body:
A coalition of Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration to block a rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards or even enter the country if they rely on public benefits.

The 22 states and D.C. are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) “public charge” rule , set to take effect Friday.

The states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), argue the rule will penalize immigrants and their families for using public benefits like food stamps, Medicaid or housing vouchers to which they are legally entitled.

“Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” James said in a statement. “This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled.”

The lawsuit argues that under the rule, immigrants would need to stop using public assistance programs to meet their basic needs or risk being denied green cards in the future.

Noncitizens and family members would disenroll from programs, even though they are eligible, and the states argued they will lose billions of dollars in federal funding.

They said the rule is “arbitrary and capricious” and that the DHS both ignored the harmful consequences of the change and failed to adequately justify it.

“As households forgo their legal access to benefits—such as preventative healthcare, nutritional assistance, and school lunch—public health, local economies, public education, and public safety will suffer. The Final Rule will increase the prevalence of disease, drive up the costs of medical care, and increase poverty,” the lawsuit argued.

A separate lawsuit challenging the rule was filed by a group of local governments, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D).

The Trump administration argues the rule is necessary to protect American taxpayers from subsidizing immigrants who may become dependent on public benefits.

The law focuses only on immigrants who are lawfully present and eligible to apply for permanent residency. Immigrants who are in the country illegally are not eligible for public benefits.

The final rule is a revival of a similar policy that the administration tried to impose during President Trump’s first term before it was met with legal challenges and later reversed by the Biden administration.

So-called “public charge” restrictions that bar immigrants from obtaining green cards if they are likely to rely on government assistance have been part of federal immigration policy for more than 140 years, but they have long focused only on cash benefit programs.

The Trump administration’s first attempt to change the rule broadened the types of benefits to include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, most Medicaid benefits and certain housing programs.

The new rule has no limits of what can be considered, saying only the DHS “will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits.”

For example, if a U.S. citizen child uses state-provided health insurance, that can be used against a noncitizen parent to deny them a green card. Officers could also count a child’s participation in a school’s free lunch program against their noncitizen parent’s application for citizenship.

“The final rule puts families in the untenable position of choosing between a U.S. citizen child’s access to healthcare, and their noncitizen parent’s ability to remain in the country,” the lawsuit argued.

The states’ suit was brought by the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Nevada, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, along with the governor of Pennsylvania.

Alongside New York City, the local lawsuit was brought by Chicago; the City and County of San Francisco; Santa Clara County, Calif.; Seattle; and King County, Wash.

articles.title: GLP-1-driven vitamin deficiency linked to rare brain disorder: Study
articles.summary: Researchers found a rare but potentially life-threatening brain disorder in a small number of people taking Ozempic, Wegovy and similar drugs.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A new study found that a rare but serious brain condition has been identified in a small number of people taking popular weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Wernicke encephalopathy is a rare neurological disorder caused by a severe deficiency of vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

Researchers identified 15 cases reported in 2023 and 2024 among people taking GLP-1 medications containing semaglutide, found in Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, found in Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Vitamin B1 is essential for proper nerve function. Without enough of it, patients can develop confusion, problems with balance and coordination, and abnormal eye movements.

If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent brain damage or death. Physicians consider it a medical emergency.

GLP-1 drugs can contribute to vitamin deficiencies by suppressing appetite and reducing food intake, including foods rich in vitamin B1, such as pork, fish and whole grains.

The study found that most patients who developed the condition also experienced severe vomiting, loss of appetite, poor nutrition or rapid weight loss.

While the disorder remains rare, researchers said the findings should help doctors educate patients about the risk and monitor for warning signs.

articles.title: Brothers rescue group of elderly people from burning California assisted living facility
articles.summary: (KTLA) — Two young brothers worked quickly to rescue a group of elderly people after a fire broke out at an assisted living facility in Glendale, Calif., on Friday. Glendale firefighters responded to the burning home on the 1800 block of Mountain Street around 4:45 p.m. As the flames grew and heavy smoke billowed from…
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Two young brothers worked quickly to rescue a group of elderly people after a fire broke out at an assisted living facility in Glendale, Calif., on Friday.

Glendale firefighters responded to the burning home on the 1800 block of Mountain Street around 4:45 p.m.

As the flames grew and heavy smoke billowed from the home, neighbors Alex Bazinyan, 20, and his brother Narek Bazinyan, 15, realized time was of the essence and decided to run over and help.

“I ran outside and I was looking at the front door when I saw the nurse outside and she was screaming for help,” Alex told Nexstar’s KTLA’s John Fenoglio.

The brothers knew several people were trapped inside the home that was operating as an assisted living facility for seniors.

Narek initially grabbed a garden hose to help quell the flames, but as the blaze grew more intense and screams for help grew louder, they knew they had to run into the fire.

“I go inside this big room and I see all these old people on the floor with catheters,” Alex recalled. “Some people were injured, had blood on their legs. We just took everybody out one by one.”

There were eight people inside the home — two nurses and six elderly residents, most of whom were unable to walk. The brothers said the nurses were desperately trying to remove the elderly residents from the home but were struggling.

“I see a guy in the back about to be engulfed by the flames,” Narek recalled when he entered the home. “The nurse is trying to pick him up. I go and grab his legs and pull him out to the front.”

Soon after, two additional neighbors also ran over to help evacuate the residents.

“As I’m looking around, I just see flames going up and coming towards me,” Narek said. “I tried bringing everyone out as fast as I could. There was smoke everywhere. I was pretty much blinded by the smoke.”

The brothers were able to safely rescue all six elderly residents and placed them on the front lawn as they awaited fire crews.

But just as they moved the last person out of the burning home, Alex recalled hearing a loud explosion.

“I heard an explosion come from the house,” he said. “I looked back and I didn’t understand what exploded, but I just heard a big boom.”

Firefighters arrived at the home and were able to extinguish the flames before any nearby houses were affected. The Glendale Fire Department chief said an oxygen tank likely exploded, which collapsed part of the home.

Seven people were transported to the hospital with minor injuries. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

As for Alex and Narek, they said their instincts just kicked in and the only thing they were focused on was quickly rescuing everyone from the burning home.

“It’s that instinct of whenever you see people in need, you want to help them out,” Alex said. “You don’t really think about who it is. We have a really tight-knit community here.”

Narek agreed, saying, “If you ever see anyone in need, you should always try to help them out as much as you can.”

articles.title: ‘All of us are going to pay’: 30% of Americans are taking out BNPL loans to pay for groceries, and it’s probably going to cost you
articles.summary: A Washington University study found that as more consumers finance their purchases, the cost of goods goes up for all.
articles.body:
In the check-out line of your local grocery store, there's a nearly one-in-three chance someone there has used an app like Klarna or Affirm to finance their purchase of produce, milk, and eggs at some point. Their use of buy now, pay later could mean your groceries are about to cost more, economists have found.

A study from the University of Washington in St. Louis, which will be published in the next issue of the Management Science journal, found that as more consumers turn to buy now, pay later to purchase their necessities, retailers may actually increase prices and slash inventory as a result.

These types of purchases have become especially appealing for smaller, but necessary shopping trips. A Lending Tree survey of more than 6,000 U.S. consumers published in July found 29% of Americans self-report using buy now, pay later loans for groceries, nearly double the 14% from two years ago.

It's all part of a bigger trend of buy now, pay later becoming an increasingly appealing option for consumers as they face an affordability crisis of increasing healthcare and childcare costs, as well as stubbornly high inflation, with 91.5 million Americans using apps like Klarna, Affirm, and Afterpay to finance purchases. Purchases with these apps grew 20% from 2021 to 2025 , according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, though they still make up only about 1% of credit card transactions.

Researchers led by Panos Kouvelis, a professor of supply chain, operations, and technology at WashU's Olin Business School, set out to find what exactly would make this model appealing to retailers, who have to pay merchant fee for each buy now, pay later transaction. The study authors developed an economic model that captured not only consumers' willingness and ability to pay for goods using buy now, pay later, but also retailers' expected profits. They found that retailers increased their sticker prices to offset the merchant fee, meaning in some cases, customers paying in-full effectively subsidized the customers who financed their purchases, and all consumers saw higher prices.

"Retailers, as a result of accepting these kinds of payments, they are going to increase prices, which basically means that all of us are going to pay for these practices that are out there," Kouvelis told Fortune .

Why buy now, pay later might sting consumers and retailers alike

Retailers are feeling this pressure to raise prices particularly because of consumers' growing reliance on loans to pay for basics like groceries. Buy now, pay later was originally intended for large discretionary purchases like furniture or gaming consoles. These products have higher margins, meaning that for the retailers selling them to consumers financing the purchase, they would still be profitable even after paying the merchant fee. Necessities like groceries, however, have much thinner margins.

articles.title: ClickFix attacks are tricking Mac and Windows users into hacking themselves | TechCrunch
articles.summary: If you clicked on a fake HBO Max ad on Reddit in the past week, you might have fallen victim to a rising "ClickFix" security threat.
articles.body:
If you clicked on an HBO Max ad on Reddit over the past week, you might want to check your computer for malware.

These so-called “ClickFix” attacks have quickly become one of the rising cybersecurity threats of 2026, and they’re getting both sneakier and compromising people’s devices with greater frequency. Until recently, ClickFix attacks were a rarity, capitalizing on people searching the web for quick tech fixes. They have since evolved into a massive international effort to hack into people’s computers.

The attacks involve fake websites, or legitimate websites that have been hacked, which display a message that appears to look like a CAPTCHA or an anti-bot checkbox. Once clicked, a prompt appears asking the user to perform a “check” to proceed, which gives instructions to copy and paste a string of text into the user’s Windows command prompt or Mac Terminal app.

As soon as the user hits return, they unwittingly and instantly install info-stealing malware on their computer, capable of immediately stealing their passwords, access to their logged-in accounts, and crypto wallets. Since the user is working in the computer’s terminal, which lets them interact directly with the operating system using text-based commands, many of these attacks evade antivirus and security defense tools.

Security researchers now say that the latest ClickFix campaign they’ve seen involved hackers posting fake ads on Reddit, linking to a page that looks like HBO Max but contains a ClickFix lure that tricks people into hacking themselves. The hackers compromised the official HBO Max’s account on Reddit that was then used to post hundreds of fake but real-looking adverts to the news-sharing site, according to security researchers at Hudson Rock and a thread on Reddit’s cybersecurity subreddit.

It’s unclear how many people clicked on these fake ads or how many were ultimately compromised as a result. Warner Brothers Discovery, which owns HBO, did not respond to a request for comment.

Reddit told TechCrunch it “recently learned that an HBO Max account authorized to run advertisements on Reddit was compromised and used to run ads containing malicious links,” and that the company locked the account and removed the ads. When asked, Reddit did not say how many users were targeted or clicked the malicious ads.

While it’s typical for developers to run one-line snippets of code in their computer’s terminal, it’s less common for regular users to use the Command Prompt or PowerShell in Windows, or the Terminal in macOS. Companies that run fleets of Windows computers can block access to these features across the entire domain to prevent them from being exploited, per security researcher Kevin Beaumont .

As noted by Ars Technica , a tool for Mac users called BlockBlock can also defend against attacks that try to trick Apple users into hacking themselves.

articles.title: Florida’s ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ confined migrants in ‘small metal enclosures’: DHS internal watchdog
articles.summary: A new report reviewing the conditions at the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” center in Florida slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to meet a variety of federal standards, describing “unprecedented” treatment of migrants, including containing them in cages about the size of a phone booth. The Monday report from the Department of Homeland…
articles.body:
A new report reviewing the conditions at the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” center in Florida slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to meet a variety of federal standards, describing “unprecedented” treatment of migrants, including containing them in cages about the size of a phone booth.

The Monday report from the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) is the first such federal review of the facility, which is referred to in the report as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF).

The report describes alarming conditions, including unhygienic practices for food and water as well as limited opportunities for migrants to bathe themselves.

OIG said Alligator Alcatraz provided half the living space for migrants required under federal law — just 28 square feet when the facility was at max capacity, far from the 75-square-foot mandate.

ICE officials also used cages that were roughly 4 feet by 4 feet as “‘calming areas’ for detainees to deescalate and have time alone.”

“FSSF confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures — each offering about 18 square feet of floor space — for periods ranging from several minutes to nearly 2 hours, a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities. The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” OIG wrote.

OIG found that in at least one documented case, a migrant was put in the small cages as a punishment.

The report generated swift blowback from immigration advocates who targeted ICE’s explanation for the small cages.

“There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike,” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of refugee settlement agency Global Refuge, said in a statement.

“The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food, and basic hygiene — and in at least one case locked in a cage as punishment. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty, carried out in our name and on our dime, to the tune of more than a million dollars a day.”

OIG said they were unable to “independently confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding their use of the enclosures” as well as other allegations, such as deprivation of food or water issues described in a prior Amnesty International report, as none of the detainees interviewed while OIG was there reported those conditions.

“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG. Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being,” the watchdog wrote.

Both ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to request for comment.

In the report, however, the agency and department placed much of the responsibility for the facility on Florida, despite it being constructed with federal funds and managed by ICE agents.

“While FEMA [Federal Emergency Management Agency] provided funding for the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF) under the Shelter and Services Program, DHS did not have a contract with Florida to manage the detention space within the facility. The State of Florida authorized the repurposing of the center from the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport into a state detention center,” DHS officials wrote in a letter in response to the report.

Other aspects also generated significant attention from inspectors.

Several detainees told OIG investigators they did not have access to clean water, saying that self-serve water stations were dirty. Migrants were also given a cup but said they had no way to wash it.

Some were also only scheduled to shower three days a week, and the report includes photos of the showers covered in bugs.

images.caption: A bus exits the “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration detention center in the Florida Everglades on May 26, 2026, in Ochopee, Fla.

articles.title: Trump weighs in on Flock debate: ‘I like them’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday backed the use of Flock cameras, a controversial surveillance tool. “Speaking of [artificial intelligence], Flock cameras. You haven’t talked a lot about these Flock cameras. A lot of law enforcement say they really help them. Would you be willing to back that?” a reporter asked Trump on Air Force One. “No,…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday backed the use of Flock cameras, a controversial surveillance tool .

“Speaking of [artificial intelligence], Flock cameras. You haven’t talked a lot about these Flock cameras. A lot of law enforcement say they really help them. Would you be willing to back that?” a reporter asked Trump on Air Force One.

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president responded , adding later, “I like them.”

Pushback to the AI vehicle surveillance systems operated by Flock Safety has grown on both sides of the aisle.

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database. That database logs license plate numbers, as well as car features like make, model, color and bumper stickers. Local jurisdictions can share data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that law enforcement can use in crime solving.

Earlier this month, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been on the president’s bad side in the last few years , unveiled a bill aimed at limiting federal funds used for automated license plate reader cameras (ALPRs) and biometric surveillance cameras.

The legislation, named the Flock-Off Act , would halt any effort to buy, install, maintain, operate or upgrade ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras for municipalities or local law enforcement.

“Federal taxpayers should not be forced to fund the surveillance state,” Massie said in a post on the social platform X, in which he discussed the bill.

articles.title: Clicked wedding invite, lost Rs2.75 lakh: Pune retired auditor falls prey to APK fraud
articles.summary: Pune: Cybercrooks stole Rs2.75 lakh from a 75-year-old retired PMC auditor via a fake online wedding invite that downloaded a remote-access APK.
articles.body: PUNE: Cybercrooks allegedly siphoned off Rs2.75 lakh from a retired auditor (75) of Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) by sending him an online wedding invitation card between Aug 31 and Sept 1.The elderly man lodged a complaint with the Kothrud police on Sunday. The retired auditor stated in his FIR that he was alone at home when he received a message on his messaging application from a number similar to his nephew’s cellphone number.He opened the message and saw an online wedding invitation card.An officer from Kothrud police said, “The retired auditor opened the wedding card and later went to sleep. Around midnight between Aug 31 and Sept 1, he started receiving messages from his bank stating Rs20,000, Rs40,000, Rs60,000 and other amounts had been withdrawn from his account. He had neither visited the bank nor an ATM, and realised that the money was being withdrawn from his bank account.”The next morning, he visited the bank and blocked his account. By then, the fraudsters had withdrawn Rs2.75 lakh from it.When he approached Pune cyberpolice, “A police officer checked his phone and found an .apk file downloaded on his cellphone. Inquiry revealed he had downloaded the .apk file by clicking on the wedding invitation card. It was a remote-access software link, and the complainant ended up sharing his banking credentials with the fraudsters after downloading it,” said an officer from the cyberpolice.On June 13 this year, a shopkeeper (53) from Tadiwala Road lodged a complaint with Bund Garden police, saying online fraudsters had siphoned off Rs5.3 lakh from his bank account by sending him an online wedding invitation.On May 21, cybercrooks sent .apk files to two different people and siphoned off money from their bank accounts. The Khadak and Faraskhana police registered two separate complaints against the online fraudsters. The two victims were cheated of a total of Rs8.5 lakh.An APK (Android Package Kit) file is the standard file format used by the Android operating system to distribute and install cellphone apps and games. Online fraudsters misuse .apk files to compromise their targets’ devices.Such files can give fraudsters remote access to a device, allowing them to monitor the cellphone or laptop. Once they obtain banking details, they siphon off money from the victims’ bank accounts.Pune cyber police have appealed to people not to download any file ending with .apk received through a message or a link. articles.title: Fed Extends Pause on Reserve Management Purchases to Mid-October
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve said Monday for the second straight month it won’t buy Treasury bills for reserve management purposes in the upcoming period, an indicati...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The Federal Reserve said Monday for the second straight month it won't buy Treasury bills for reserve management purposes in the upcoming period, an indication that policymakers are comfortable with the level of bank reserves in the financial system.

While the New York Fed's open markets desk doesn't plan on conducting reserve management purchases over the monthly period ending Oct. 14, it still plans on buying about $15.6 billion in reinvestment purchases over the time, according to its website.

The hiatus signals the Fed is confident in the smooth functioning of funding markets. That's borne out with the Secured Overnight Financing Rate — a benchmark rate based on the cost of borrowing against Treasury securities — trading at or below the interest on reserve balances rate, or IORB, for most of the past month, as well as the Treasury Department's paydown of bill supply ahead of the quarterly tax deadline. The change doesn't signal any shift in monetary policy or balance-sheet strategy.

Wall Street strategists from Wells Fargo and Bank of America expected RMPs to be on hiatus this month before resuming in mid-October in anticipation of pockets of pressure in the funding markets that are expected to surface when Treasury ramps up bill issuance beginning next month. Barclays Plc strategist Samuel Earl sees purchases moving back up to $10 billion in October and $20 billion in November.

Citigroup Inc. strategists, however, see the Fed remaining on pause for the rest of the year, noting that bank reserve balances have already been pushed back to a "lightly abundant regime."

Bank reserves stood at $3.04 trillion as of Sept. 9. That's up from $2.85 trillion at the end of last year and above the year-to-date average of $3.01 trillion.

The Fed abruptly stopped shrinking its balance sheet — a process known as quantitative tightening — at the end of 2025 and pivoted to adding reserves back into the financial system by buying short-term Treasuries due in less than a year.

In December, the central bank began buying about $40 billion of bills each month in a bid to ease the pressures that were building in short-term rates. At that time, then-Chair Jerome Powell said the Fed was "front-loading" its purchases to ensure there were enough reserves through the April tax season.

articles.title: RFK Jr. to headline Children’s Health Defense conference in DC
articles.summary: Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is scheduled to give a keynote address this week at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine advocacy organization he co-founded and led prior to becoming head of the nation’s health agency. For the past year Kennedy has worked to distance himself from the efforts…
articles.body:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is scheduled to give a keynote address this week at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine advocacy organization he co-founded and led prior to becoming head of the nation’s health agency.

For the past year Kennedy has worked to distance himself from the efforts of Children’s Health Defense, a group that questions the safety and efficacy of childhood vaccines and is a leading force of the anti-vaccination movement.

During his Senate confirmation hearing in January 2025, Kennedy sought to reassure lawmakers that he would not undermine public confidence in vaccines and maintained he was not anti-vaccine.

During one memorable exchange, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) displayed images of baby onesies sold by the anti-vaccine organization that read “Unvaxxed, Unafraid” and “No Vax, No Problem.”

“Are you supportive of these onesies?” Sanders asked.

Kennedy said he had nothing to do with the merchandise and noted he had resigned from the group.

“I am supportive of vaccines,” Kennedy said at the time.

Thursday’s conference in Washington, D.C., marks Kennedy’s first appearance at an official Children’s Health Defense conference since he joined the Trump administration, but the group now wields significant political clout.

Kennedy did not attend the group’s national conference last year.

Leaders of the organization have been hired in prominent positions at HHS, and views that were once considered fringe — like a false and debunked link between vaccines and autism — have become mainstream in the Trump administration, oftentimes echoed by President Trump himself.

HHS did not immediately return a request for comment.

Thursday’s event is touted as a way to “highlight the work of key government officials and individuals who are advocating for transparency, accountability and justice in the area of public health.”

It comes amid unprecedented efforts by Trump and HHS to roll back childhood vaccines and downplay the severity of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks — notably measles.

Aside from Kennedy, the event will feature speeches from lawmakers including Republican Sens. Ron Johnson (Wis.) and Rand Paul (Ky.), as well as GOP Reps. Paul Gosar (Ariz.) and Thomas Massie (Ky.).

The event will also feature Andrew Wakefield, a doctor whose medical license was revoked and who is credited with starting the argument that modern vaccines cause autism.

Kennedy joined the World Mercury Project, a nonprofit that pressed to remove mercury from vaccines in 2015. He rebranded it as Children’s Health Defense and served as its chair and top lawyer until 2024, when he stepped down to run for president.

He earned a six-figure salary at the organization and millions more helping to sue vaccine makers and challenge state-level vaccine policies.

The group promotes anti-immunization views as part of its goal to end chronic health conditions in children by “eliminating toxic exposures.”

articles.body:
Political figures across the aisle, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon, are finding themselves on the same side of a growing fight over AI regulations.

Sanders and Bannon are among a handful of political leaders speaking at a Tuesday event advocating controls to keep humans in charge of AI.

The Pro-Human Assembly, hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute in Washington, D.C., comes as the district scrambles to address the risks and safety concerns growing around AI.

Concerns were supercharged last week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and claimed in a post on the social platform that researchers at the frontier labs “believe AI could kill all humans” but push forward anyway.

Coxon warned superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance — could destroy all of humanity if the technology’s development does not slow down.

Sanders is one of the loudest voices on the left calling for AI regulations. He and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) called for a permanent ban on the development and deployment of superintelligence in the wake of recent hackings involving “rogue” models.

Bannon has taken a populist approach to AI, repeatedly warning about the risks of AI and data centers used to power the technology’s development.

Other speakers include Casar, Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Reps. Chip Roy (R-Texas), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Don Beyer (D-Va.) and New York State Assembly member Alex Bores, who ran a congressional campaign advocating for better oversight of AI model development.

While Democrats and Republicans remain far apart on how to regulate the technology, a growing number of lawmakers agree more needs to be done to ensure AI is developed safely, with the country’s labor workforce in mind.

President Trump, an ally of Bannon, is doubling down on his support for the AI and data center industry. He argued in a Monday post on Truth Social that the only protections needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” claiming the government has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI firms already.

articles.title: Jensen Huang puts Trump on speakerphone onstage to announce robots won’t take over the world
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a call from President Trump on Monday while onstage at an event, and the president launched into his take on recent fears about AI development.
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a call from President Trump on Monday while onstage at the All-In Podcast’s All-In Summit. It’s not the first time Huang has taken a call from the president during work, but this time he put Trump on speakerphone before a big crowd. During the call, the president launched into his take on recent fears about AI development, which he called a “hoax,” and told the crowd that “the robots will not be taking over.” It’s already a frothy week for AI news. The call with the president followed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s long essay published this weekend titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” where he argued for slowing down AI development and coordination between governments. The essay sparked many responses from AI executives, who generally agreed. But Trump pushed back in Truth Social posts on Monday and repurposed some of what he said in those posts at the event. Heard onstage, Trump also commented on data centers, claiming there would be communities that would be “dying” without data centers but were now “really wealthy” (though without providing specifics). Huang did not push back, saying instead that “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.” Huang also appealed to Trump by telling him he was speaking to “thousands” of people. articles.body:
Oil prices on Monday leaped more than 4 percent after Yemen-based militant Houthis struck Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure and ships, leaving one crucial pipeline out of service for weeks.

The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent crude , settled at $105.66 per barrel as of Monday afternoon. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) , the benchmark in the U.S., rose to $101.28.

The average price of gas in the U.S. reached $4.32, a 7-cent increase since last week, and the average price for diesel reached $6.23, a new record, both according to data from AAA .

Saudi Arabia’s 745-mile-long East-West Pipeline has helped the government move crude production from the Persian Gulf ports to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, where tankers can export oil.

Saudi officials familiar with the Thursday attack on the pipeline told the Associated Press that it could take 3-5 weeks to repair, though it could partially work while crews work to fix it. The pipeline moved a weekly average of 2.6 million to 4 million barrels a day since late August.

The Norway-based energy analyst Rystad Energy said Monday that the increase in the price of Brent crude “is a clear signal that the market is increasingly pricing in a significant loss of supply.”

The Houthis, a proxy of the Iranian regime, entered the U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran to retaliate against Gulf state attacks on Iran after calling on Persian Gulf countries, the U.S. and Israel to seek a path to diplomacy and peace with Iran. They warned that they would retaliate if the conflict escalated.

The Houthis also captured the crucial islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, which are both located 100 miles north of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to Saudi Arabia’s key Asian markets. The islands are also 20 miles from a U.S. military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa.

The rebels also took over the port city of Mokha, another Red Sea port crucial to shipping, risking opening up a new front in the Iran war. The Saudis have reportedly urged President Trump to launch strikes on the Houthis, while the U.S. has sent more than 100 advisors to help the Saudis in their fight with the rebel forces.

Oil exports through the Red Sea after passing through the East-West Pipeline have been an alternative to exporting oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian regime has effectively cut off the transit of oil out of the region in response to U.S. strikes, causing gas and oil prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have soared to record highs as Ukraine carries out its drone strikes on Russian refineries . Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to call off further attacks on these refineries.

“He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

articles.title: Trump guts climate rules for coal and gas power plants
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Monday gutted regulations that limited planet-warming emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants. The move allows a sector that makes up a large share of the U.S.’s climate change contributions to release greenhouse gases unchecked by the government. It’s expected to be a win for the fossil fuel industry, while allowing…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday gutted regulations that limited planet-warming emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants.

The move allows a sector that makes up a large share of the U.S.’s climate change contributions to release greenhouse gases unchecked by the government. It’s expected to be a win for the fossil fuel industry, while allowing the release of significantly more planet-heating pollution.

When it proposed to kill the regulations entirely last year, the Trump administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, this would result in the release of 123 million more metric tons of carbon dioxide, equivalent to putting an additional 28.7 million gas-powered cars on the road.

Monday’s move could be slightly different. While it is expected to repeal large swaths of Biden-era power plant regulations, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) assistant administrator Aaron Szabo told reporters that limited pieces of Biden- and Obama-era regs would remain in place.

In addition to Monday’s final rule, the EPA proposed to find that the Clean Air Act does not give it the authority to regulate power plant emissions due to their climate impacts. If finalized, Szabo said that this move could block future administrations from regulating power plants’ climate emissions.

Overall, he said that the moves would allow “American families and businesses experience lower electricity costs … thanks to an increased power supply.”

The moves come as high electricity demand and increasing power prices continue to be a major political issue. Last year’s analysis found that in 2035, axing power plant climate rules could reduce electricity prices by an average of 1.4 percent.

In a press release, the EPA said that it expects its final rule to save $310 billion.

President Trump has falsely said that climate change is a “hoax” on multiple occasions, and his administration has broadly sought to cut back or eliminate climate regulations. It recently repealed all climate rules for cars and trucks , saying their emissions did not pose a threat to the public.

Climate change has been linked to worsening heat waves and extreme weather. The U.S. power sector is a major driver of planet-warming emissions, responsible for a quarter of total U.S. emissions.

A report from New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity found that if the U.S. power sector were a country, it would be the world’s sixth-largest emitter, contributing more to climate change than the entirety of nations such as Canada, Japan, Brazil and Mexico.

The report also said that the sector’s 2022 emissions alone will contribute to future climate change impacts that are expected to cause about 5,300 additional premature deaths in the U.S. due to heat and wildfire smoke.

“The public health and welfare toll of this deregulation is just going to be staggering,” said Jason Schwartz, one of the report’s authors and regulatory policy director at the Institute, told The Hill.

Environmental activists recoiled at the Trump administration’s latest rollback before news of it was officially announced.

“It’s really just the Trump EPA putting their head in the sand,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “I mean, you can look at the weather we experienced this summer, the heat waves on the Fourth of July. We’re going into an El Niño season with potential hurricanes and even more extreme weather. We see the impacts of climate change all around us every day, and the Trump EPA is trying to say, ‘Well, that’s not our problem.'”

Meanwhile, industry players celebrated the move.

Rachael Marsh, chief legal officer at the Edison Electric Institute, a trade group representing power companies, said in a statement that it “welcomes EPA’s repeal” of the Biden-era rule.

Rich Nolan, president and CEO of the National Mining Association, which represents the coal industry, said in a statement that the Trump rule “has averted what would have been a catastrophic collision of unlawful and unworkable Biden-era technology mandates with surging energy demands.”

“With today’s repeal, well-operating coal plants are no longer faced with the false choice between commercially unavailable and technically infeasible technologies, fuel-switching or closure. The administration’s action corrects the egregious misuse of the Clean Air Act as a political tool to end American coal generation and implements the law as Congress intended,” Nolan added.

The EPA’s action repeals most of a Biden-era rule that would have required existing coal plants and new gas plants to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

articles.title: Trump throws out power plant climate pollution rules
articles.summary: The Trump administration wants to eliminate any limits to greenhouse gas pollution from power plants as it prioritizes making the US “the AI capital of the world.”
articles.body: The Environmental Protection Agency announced its plans today to kill any remaining standards on how much greenhouse gas pollution power plants are allowed to emit in the US. The move will only make electricity dirtier as AI, electric vehicles, and a revival of domestic manufacturing drive up power demand. The EPA’s proposal today is a major escalation of President Donald Trump’s efforts to promote fossil fuels while making it easier to build out energy-hungry data centers. Environmental and consumer advocates, meanwhile, are fighting back — arguing that Trump’s deregulation spree comes with higher costs for the environment, public health, and Americans’ pocketbooks. “Failure to limit climate pollution means more children ending up in the emergency room with asthma attacks and heatstroke, more families struggling to rebuild homes after harrowing storms,” Moms Clean Air Force director and cofounder Dominique Browning said in an emailed statement. “It means higher health care bills, higher insurance costs, and more economic struggle at a time when Americans cannot afford it.” The power sector pumps out a quarter of the nation’s greenhouse gas emissions, surpassed only by transportation. In February, the Trump administration overturned the “endangerment finding” for vehicles. The finding recognized that greenhouse gases “threaten the public health and welfare of current and future generations” and allowed the agency to regulate that pollution under the Clean Air Act. Now, the EPA is extending that rollback to power plants. There is scientific consensus that greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels causes climate change. But in its press release today, the EPA argues that greenhouse gas pollution is “out of its scope to regulate” because its impacts are “global in nature, and any potential public health harms are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the U.S. power sector.” The US has produced more greenhouse gas pollution than any other country in history and is still a leading carbon emitter after China. The agency today is finalizing its repeal of Biden-era greenhouse gas requirements for power plants, as well as proposing the elimination of any remaining limits to that climate pollution for the power sector. The EPA claims the finalized rule would save $310 billion while the additional proposed actions would shave off $370 million “in direct compliance costs.” Energy, of course, has become a flashpoint in the culture war over affordability. Electricity has gotten more expensive in the US as demand rises for the first time in over a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into power grids. At the same time, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin has prioritized making America “the AI capital of the world,” ostensibly by slashing environmental regulations for energy-intensive data centers and the gas and coal-fired plants that power them. The EPA’s proposed changes will be open for public comment for 45 days, and are likely to face a raft of legal challenges. “The Sierra Club will fight back against this reckless and dangerous proposal with everything we have in the courts, in Congress, and in communities across the country,” Sierra Club chief program officer Holly Bender said in an emailed press statement. “While wildfires rage, floods devastate communities, and families struggle to afford skyrocketing electricity bills and insurance premiums, the Trump administration is handing the fossil fuel industry a license to keep polluting.”

articles.title: Jeffries calls on Congress to stay in Washington to address AI concerns
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is calling on House GOP leaders to remain in Washington to allow Congress to consider new limits on AI companies following dire warnings from industry insiders about the threat the technology poses to humanity. Speaking to reporters Monday in the Capitol, Jeffries said the calls for a slowdown from…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is calling on House GOP leaders to remain in Washington to allow Congress to consider new limits on AI companies following dire warnings from industry insiders about the threat the technology poses to humanity.

Speaking to reporters Monday in the Capitol, Jeffries said the calls for a slowdown from within the industry should be a wakeup call for lawmakers in the Capitol, who have dabbled at the edges of AI regulation for years without taking any significant steps to ensure public safety.

Jeffries did not promote specific reforms, but urged Congress to delay its long, pre-election recess “until something is done decisively to protect the safety and the well-being of the American people.”

“Republicans have completely abandoned their responsibility to legislate and engage in public policy efforts in a responsible fashion in the area of artificial intelligence,” Jeffries said.

The pressure is unlikely to bear fruit. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) opposes any swift action on new AI regulations, warning that hasty new limits risk overburdening American technology companies to the benefit of America’s global adversaries.

“The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and in hyperregulation,” Johnson told reporters Monday in the Capitol. “If you do that, then you lose your edge.”

Johnson has scheduled the House to adjourn on Thursday and remain in recess through the Nov. 3 elections.

Still, the public anxieties surrounding AI — and the related issue of data centers, which are helping to fuel the AI boom — have increasingly become campaign fodder heading into the midterms, when both the House and Senate are up for grabs.

The issue reached new heights over the weekend when three top leaders in the AI industry — Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman — urged a more cautious approach to the development of the technology. A failure to do so, Amodei, the head of Anthropic, warned in a long blog post , could lead to global catastrophe.

President Trump has come out strongly in favor of data centers and against regulating AI — two positions that put him at odds with the majority of voters. And Democrats are highlighting both topics to portray the president and other GOP leaders as out of touch with public sentiment heading to the polls.

“They’re not really concerned about over-regulation. They want no regulation,” Jeffries said. “And that’s the height of irresponsibility.”

Jeffries noted that, in the previous Congress, he and former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) had launched an AI task force designed to balance the success of American AI companies with public safety precautions. The panel did not survive the transition into the new Congress — a development Jeffries blamed on Trump’s return to the White House.

“Republicans in this Congress, at the direction of Donald Trump, detonated that bipartisan effort and endangered the health and the safety and the well-being of the American people in doing so,” he said.
