articles.title: Costco nearly doubles cost of motor oil, limits purchases
articles.summary: A price hike and purchase limits may take you back to the days of empty shelves where toilet paper once stood, but this likely won’t impact you as much as you may immediately fear.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — Costco may have cut the prices for several popular items earlier this year, but it’s now raising the cost and limiting the sale of another: motor oil.

Costco’s Kirkland Signature full-synthetic motor oil 5-quart two pack now costs around $58, well above the approximately $30 it had been selling for just last year, and limiting customers to buying two boxes a week. It is also limiting purchases of Mobil 1’s full-synthetic motor oil 1-quart six pack, which sells for about $44, to five per membership.

A price hike and purchase limits may take you back to the days of empty shelves where toilet paper once stood , but this likely won’t impact you as much as you may immediately fear.

Unless you’re responsible for “a fleet of thousands of cars,” you probably don’t have to worry about it much, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, told Nexstar.

“The normal car requires four to five quarts every 5,000 miles or so,” De Haan said, describing Costco’s limit as “what would be an extremely reasonable amount.”

It is, however, indicative of a larger picture: high oil prices.

De Haan told Nexstar that oil prices have reached their highest level in months. He pointed to attacks in the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline in Saudi Arabia, as well as Ukrainian drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, as contributing to the price hikes. The Saudi oil pipeline will mostly be out of service for weeks following an attack last week, two regional officials told The Associated Press.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude went above $109 on Monday morning.

“As you would expect, everything derived from a barrel of oil is being impacted in different ways,” De Haan said.

While Costco’s motor oil price hikes and sale limits may not impact you much, you may continue to feel pressure at the pump, especially if you drive a diesel vehicle.

The national average for a gallon of regular gasoline, as of Sept. 14, is $4.31, according to AAA . That’s well over the $3.17 per gallon average reported at this time last year.

Diesel, meanwhile, set a record on Monday, with a national average of $6.23, per AAA data. At this time last year, the national average was just under $3.70 per gallon.

Prices at the pump for diesel and regular gasoline closely follow that of crude oil .

With oil prices continuing to rise due to ongoing tension in the Middle East, oil companies stand to profit more from turning refined crude oil into diesel or gasoline than motor oil.

It remains to be seen if other motor oil retailers like Walmart, Amazon and AutoZone will boost their prices or set purchase limits. Walmart, Amazon and AutoZone did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters he would like to see the Protect College Sports Act, the proposed landmark legislation regulating the big business of college sports, signed by President Trump live on ESPN’s “College GameDay.” “Our goal from the beginning was not just to squeak by with 60 votes but to get a big…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters he would like to see the Protect College Sports Act, the proposed landmark legislation regulating the big business of college sports, signed by President Trump live on ESPN’s “College GameDay.”

“Our goal from the beginning was not just to squeak by with 60 votes but to get a big bipartisan vote. We got that in committee, which surprised a lot of observers,” Cruz said during a press conference outside the Capitol on Monday. “I’ve spoken with House leadership in the last week and if we get a big bipartisan vote, it goes into the House with a lot of momentum … and the president is ready to sign it.”

Cruz grinned as he floated an unusual venue for the president to sign the legislation should it pass both chambers of Congress.

“I’ve actually suggested that he sign it on ‘College Gameday,’ on campus, which truly would be a remarkable moment,” the senator said, in reference to ESPN’s popular college football pregame show. “We’ve gotta get there first, but it would be an amazing victory for student athletes if we can get that done.”

The bipartisan group of lawmakers has been telegraphing confidence in the bill’s chances for weeks, pointing to recent controversies in college football and basketball regarding player eligibility and compensation as evidence the “wild west” of college sports needs to be better regulated.

The sweeping bipartisan legislation would grant the NCAA and its member schools limited antitrust protection shielding it from litigation around issues like the transfer portal, revenue sharing and student-athlete compensation through name, image and likeness endorsement deals.

Trump has endorsed the Protect College Sports Act, following the formation of a White House Task Force on College Sports earlier this year and an executive order he signed with language that closely mirrors key points of the Protect College Sports Act.

Some of the bill’s backers have expressed worry that Trump’s attachment to the bill could hurt its chances with Democrats before the midterm elections this fall.

“The president is enthusiastic, but he’s also given space in the Senate to let the coalition come together,” Cruz said. “With some senators, the president’s endorsement is more helpful than with others. That’s the nature of politics, and he understands that.”

Monday’s presser came just days after Cruz appeared on “College GameDay” to advocate with the bill, during which he was met with boos from fans at the University of Texas as he spoke extensively about the legislation.

Legendary Alabama coach Nick Saban, also a co-host of ESPN’s “College GameDay,” is one of the bill’s most prominent backers.

Critics of the College Sports Act, including Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), contend the bill hands the NCAA and top universities too much power and will limit the earning potential of most student athletes, particularly at nonrevenue-generating and Olympic sports.

Some conservative members in the Senate, meanwhile, have expressed concern about the bill’s ramifications relating to transgender athletes, particularly in states where they are banned from competition.

A vote on the bill, authored by Cruz and Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), is expected as soon as Tuesday, though the lawmakers said Monday it could be pushed to next week depending on how efforts to whip votes in the upper chamber progress this week.

U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Gulf countries suffered around $184 million in estimated damages from Iranian military strikes, a new Pentagon watchdog report found.

The posts are located in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the Pentagon watchdog said in the 44-page report , the first one since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in late February.

The heaviest damage was sustained in Iraq with over $157 million, followed by Kuwait with more than $14 million in damages and $11.5 million in Saudi Arabia, the report said. The State Department, meanwhile, reported that as of June 2, it had incurred $113 million in costs related to the war and “as it continues to assess damage, costs are likely to rise.”

In addition, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and some 800 wounded in the more than six-month war. About 50,000 American troops are still deployed to the region, with the Trump administration yet to provide a clear exit strategy from the deeply unpopular conflict.

Top administration officials have at times downplayed the damages Iranian one-way attack drones and missiles have inflicted on U.S. military bases, aircraft and other assets in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) theater.

Last week, President Trump denied news reports that several U.S. military jets were damaged in Iran’s attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.

“None whatsoever. No damage. No nothing,” the president said in an interview with The Hill’s sister network NewsNation when asked about one A-10 Thunderbolt losing a wing and eight F-15s sustained light damage.

More than 50 U.S. aircraft have been damaged or destroyed since the Iran war began, according to the watchdog’s report, including 4 F-15Es, seven KC-135 refueling aircraft, four AH-6 helicopters and at least 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones.

But some top officials were more candid.

“They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” the acting U.S. Navy secretary Hung Cao said in an interview last week with The Epoch Times when asked about the level of damage Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NASB), which serves as the headquarters for U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the U.S. Fifth Fleet, had sustained since the conflict began.

The Navy has used the NASB as its main logistics hub in the Middle East. The service branch is weighing what to do with the base, including if it should be repaired.

“I have a task force that’s looking at that,” Cao said.

articles.title: US 10-Year Treasury Yields Rise to Highest Level Since 2007
articles.summary: The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest level in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by surging energ...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest level in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by surging energy prices, mounting debt and inflation.

The yield rose as much as four basis points to 5.02% on Tuesday, surpassing a peak from 2023 to hit the highest since 2007. The latest leg of the move followed an increase in global oil prices as risks to Middle East supplies grow.

The bond slump raises the stakes ahead of the Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision on Wednesday, where investors expect officials to raise short-term borrowing costs for the first time since July 2023. If they don't hike, or if Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh signals less monetary tightening in coming months than what's priced in by money markets, then bond investors may demand even higher yields to protect against inflationary risks.

"It would be very difficult for the Fed to leave rates unchanged this week without eroding its inflation-fighting credibility," said Vail Hartman, a strategist at BMO Capital Markets. "The market is vulnerable to not only an unexpected hold, but also a dovish hike that entails a more patient takeaway from the dot-plot or press conference."

Bond yields have been rising globally since the US and Israel launched an assault on Iran in late February, disrupting the supply of Middle Eastern oil and gas. That's on top of other factors such as massive corporate borrowing to fund artificial intelligence spending, which is both flooding markets with debt and pumping stimulus into an already resilient US economy.

It also comes as the amount of debt governments issue continues to rise, both to refinance maturing bonds and to fund deficit spending. Central banks are no longer hoovering up government bonds as part of their quantitative easing programs, and demand from other traditional buyers is cooling — resulting in a greater reliance on more price-sensitive investors.

"The scope for long-end yields to fall is somewhat limited given that we don't see signs of weakness in the real economy and supply/dynamics in the Treasury market are very different relative to 2007," Phoebe White, head of US rates strategy at UBS Group AG, said via email. "Structural demand for US Treasuries, particularly among foreign official investors, is materially weaker."

articles.title: Internet shutdown crosses 100 days in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
articles.summary: Mobile data, broadband services suspended in the territory since protests calling for electoral reform in June.
articles.body:
Internet access has been severely restricted in Pakistan-administered Kashmir for more than 100 days.

Mobile data and broadband services have been suspended in the territory since protests for electoral reform erupted in early June. In response to the unrest, staggered elections were held over three rounds, with the final phase taking place on August 10. However, the partial internet shutdown continues to disrupt everyday life despite the formation of the new government.

Access to websites and apps used for online banking remains unavailable, affecting business activity across the region. The shutdown has also disrupted the academic year for students, with the government postponing entrance exams.

The partial internet blackout has continued since June 5, said NetBlocks, an independent observer that monitors internet shutdowns.

The unrest began in the lead-up to local elections scheduled for July 27.

Kashmir is a disputed region fully claimed by both India and Pakistan. Pakistan-administered Kashmir is governed under a semi-autonomous system, with its own prime minister and legislative assembly made up of 45 seats in total, including 12 reserved for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir who live in other parts of Pakistan.

On June 5, authorities banned the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKJAAC), a grassroots umbrella organisation that demanded the removal of the 12 seats in the legislature.

Authorities imposed an internet shutdown on June 5 and cracked down on protests violently, culminating in deadly clashes on July 27.

Residents and local estimates say the death toll has surpassed 50, including seven law enforcement personnel, though the figures could not be independently verified.

Voting did not take place in certain protest strongholds for security reasons, but the government was formed based on the election results from the rest of the autonomous region.

articles.title: Apple rolls out its biggest iPhone software update of 2026: 10 ways iOS 27 will 'change' your iPhone
articles.summary: Tech News News: Apple has released iOS 27, the largest iPhone software update it has shipped all year, and it is free for every iPhone 11 and newer. The rollout start.
articles.body: Apple has released iOS 27, the largest iPhone software update it has shipped all year, and it is free for every iPhone 11 and newer. The rollout started on Monday and the update is live in India now. The headline is Siri AI, a rebuilt assistant that holds a proper back and forth, reads what is on your screen, and searches your own mail, messages and photos before it answers. Underneath that sit a Camera app that can read a restaurant bill, a Shortcuts app you can talk into shape, a Photos editor that pushes a picture past its own borders, and a slider for everyone who spent the last year quietly resenting Liquid Glass.Siri AI is also the feature Apple has owed its users since 2024. The personalised, context aware assistant it demonstrated that year never shipped on schedule, and the gap was long enough that a fair number of iPhone owners stopped waiting and installed a chatbot instead. What arrives today is that promise, delivered late and still carrying a beta label, with English first and French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish following in October. Apple has hedged the rest of the release accordingly. A great deal of engineering in iOS 27 has gone into things that have nothing to do with AI, from app launch times to how the phone hands over between Wi-Fi and cellular, which is the part of this update that will reach the most people.iOS 27 compatible iPhones: the list stretches back to 2019iOS 27 installs on:iPhone 11, 11 Pro and 11 Pro MaxThe complete iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 lines, including the 16e and 17eiPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone DuoiPhone SE, second generation onwardApple Intelligence and Siri AI need a shorter list: iPhone 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max, every iPhone 16 model and later, the iPhone Air and the iPhone Duo. A handful of features sit on an even narrower shelf. Tuning how Siri sounds, down to pitch and pace, is restricted to the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, Duo, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max and Air.How to update to iOS 27Back up first through Settings, your name, iCloud Backup, Back Up Now. Use a computer instead if your iCloud storage has run out.Open Settings, General, Software Update. Swipe down on the page if iOS 27 is not showing yet.Select iOS 27 and follow the prompts. A number of users have watched the installer describe itself as 26.7 before the phone reboots onto iOS 27.Switch Siri AI on afterwards in Settings. It stays off until you ask for it, and it is not available to anyone under 13.Siri AI knows what is in your inbox, and answers from itThe new assistant works like a chatbot with one thing no rival has, which is private access to what is already on the phone. When you install the update it indexes your calendar invites, mail, texts, files and notes, then answers from that. Ask for a recent photo of your dog and it surfaces several. Ask which weekend you were in Goa and it knows, because your boarding passes told it. The working list includes:Finding a mail, message, photo, link or file by person, date or placeBuilding a home automation from an instruction such as locking every door at midnightAdding a birthday or a second number to a contact without opening the appLifting every ingredient off a recipe page into a shopping listAnswering questions about whatever is on screen, and searching the web when it has toSay the wake word and a shimmering orb appears in the Dynamic Island with a card you can pull down into a full Siri app, which keeps your conversations and continues them on an iPad. It now asks which part of a request it did not follow rather than failing silently. It is still slower to respond than Gemini, and it fumbles retrievals a well indexed inbox should make easy.Point the camera at a restaurant bill and Siri splits itSwipe past Photo and Video in the Camera app and a Siri tab appears. Hold it over a nutrition label and the numbers go into Health. Hold it over a shopfront and ask for the hours. Hold it over an event schedule and each entry lands in your calendar. The demo everyone will run is the receipt split, which reads the bill, works out each person's share with tax and tip, and settles the total through Apple Cash. Printed receipts scan reliably. Handwriting is a gamble. The Apple Cash requirement also means this is a feature Indian users can admire and not use.Write with Siri copies your tone before it writes a wordSiri can draft inside any text field, rewrite what you have typed, shift the register, or tell you where a draft is weak. In Messages and Mail it reads your existing writing and imitates your phrasing and punctuation, which is the difference between a useful draft and one you delete. Grammar suggestions now appear alongside spelling corrections across the system.Older iPhones feel quicker, and Liquid Glass gets a dialApple's own testing puts app launches up to 30 per cent faster, newly shot photos loading up to 70 per cent faster in the library, and AirDrop transfers up to 80 per cent faster. Treat the figures as the company's, but the change registers within minutes, and it lands on every supported handset instead of only the Apple Intelligence tier. Messages retries a failed send by itself now, and the switch between Wi-Fi and cellular is less jarring. For the look of the thing, Settings, Appearance, Liquid Glass opens a slider that runs from ultra clear to fully tinted.Shortcuts builds the automation from one sentenceShortcuts has always been capable and almost nobody used it, because building anything meant stacking actions by hand and guessing at the logic. Now you tap the plus sign, write what you want, and the app assembles it. Message a family member your ETA when you leave the office, or trigger a playlist when CarPlay connects. You can refine the result in plain language or edit the steps yourself.Photos can extend a shot past the edges of the frameClean Up has been the softest of Apple's editing tools since it launched, mostly because it left warped patches behind. It now runs in three modes: Fast, on device, for small removals, High Quality, which goes to Apple's servers, and Auto. Beside it are Extend, which invents what lies past the original frame, and Spatial Reframing, which shifts the apparent camera position after the picture was taken. Image Playground handles photorealistic output now, and Apple has said SynthID watermarking support is coming later this year.Safari watches a product page and tells you when the price fallsNotify Me is the smartest small idea in this release. Find the listing in Safari, open the Tab bar menu, tap Notify Me, describe the change you are waiting for and set how often the browser should check. It watches the page for a restock or a price cut and alerts you. Safari also sorts open tabs into topics on its own, and will write a custom extension from a plain description, from a citation generator to forcing a minimum font size on a site with unreadable type.AirPods finally get a custom EQ, alarms get their own volumeYou can tune the lows, mids and highs on AirPods yourself rather than accepting Apple's preset, through AirPods settings, Audio and Routing, Equaliser, Custom. It works on AirPods 4 and 5, AirPods Pro 2 and 3, and AirPods Max 2. Separately, Settings, Sounds and Haptics lets you unlink alarm volume from ringer volume, which fixes the old problem of sleeping through an alarm or being startled by a notification at maximum volume. GymKit also arrives on iPhone, and AirPods Pro 3 can pass heart rate data into a workout.A child now has to ask before opening a new websiteThe parental controls are the most substantial non AI work in this release, and they are built around approval rather than blocking:Ask to Buy holds every app install until a parent says yesAsk to Browse does the same for new websites in Safari, with the request arriving in the parent's MessagesCommunication Safety, which already caught nudity, now intervenes on gore and violence in shared images and videoTime Allowances cap daily use across Entertainment, Games and Social Media, with age guidance Apple developed with clinical and child development specialists, while Schedules decide which apps work at which hoursScreen Time itself has been redesigned around an at a glance view of what a child actually used.One phone number across two iPhones, for a monthly feeTwo iPhones running iOS 27 can share a single number, with the line following whichever handset you unlock. It is set up in Settings, Cellular, This iPhone and Another. The obstacle is the carrier. Only T-Mobile supports it at launch, at roughly Rs 440 a month, with Verizon expected later this year and no Indian operator involved yet.The smaller iOS 27 changes are the ones you will stumble intoSome of the best work in this update never made a slide. These are the fixes that remove a daily irritation rather than add a headline, and most of them land on older iPhones too.Save a single frame from a video as a photo, instead of screenshotting and cropping it. Anyone who shoots video of moving children or pets has wanted this for years.A Captured By Me filter in Photos separates pictures you actually took from the flood of forwards in your library, reaching back across older iPhones.Wallet builds a pass from a photograph of a physical card, so a library card or a gift voucher stops living in a drawer. There is a manual template route if your iPhone does not support Apple Intelligence.Home screen widgets stretch to an extra large size, which makes Notes, Calendar and Weather worth reading rather than tapping through. Weather now shows nine days instead of five.Choose which eight controls sit above the Camera viewfinder. Lens Aperture and Shutter Speed are reserved for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.Messages stops holding up your next text while a large photo crawls out over weak cellular.The bigger leftovers come with conditions attached. Call Context surfaces a confirmation code or a booking reference from your mail while you are on a call to a business. HomeKit Secure Video cameras record and stream in 4K, and the Home app can describe what happened in a clip or search footage in plain language, although those AI pieces need a 2TB iCloud+ plan for a single camera and more beyond that. Maps Flyover renders architectural detail and individual trees from aerial imagery. Cycle Tracking in Health adds perimenopause support, with deviation notifications aimed at users over 40. iCloud Shared Albums allow full resolution sharing at last, and are easier to join from Android or Windows. VoiceOver and Magnifier both pick up substantial accessibility work.One to wait for rather than look for: the Passwords app will update weak or compromised logins on your behalf, but Apple has marked that as coming in a future release rather than shipping it today.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: US Yield Surge Adds to Bessent’s Grow-Our-Way-Out Debt Challenge
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has insisted faster economic growth can wipe away concerns about troubling fiscal trajectories, a key theme of his recent G2...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has insisted faster economic growth can wipe away concerns about troubling fiscal trajectories, a key theme of his recent G20 leadership. History suggests otherwise.

Ahead of hosting the Group of 20 major world economies, Bessent said in August that "global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt." With US federal spending restraint and "3% growth, we grow our way out of this," he reiterated last week at a Texas event.

As recently as 2023 and 2024, the US was clocking near-3% growth rates, after adjusting for inflation. Yet debt held by the public climbed by roughly 10% and 7% respectively in those years — fueled by annual deficits topping $1.6 trillion — and debt as a share of economic output rose.

Back in the late 1990s, when US gross domestic product sustained gains of more than 4%, a dramatic turn to fiscal surpluses came alongside higher taxes and slower defense spending in a post-Cold War world.

Today, those dynamics are flipped. Tax rates are much lower after multiple waves of Republican-led reductions, and lawmakers from both parties in recent years have generally voted to raise, not lower, federal spending. An aging population is boosting outlays in giant entitlement programs. And amid geopolitical tensions, President Donald Trump wants Congress to approve $1.5 trillion in defense spending, a 44% boost.

"You can't grow your way out of it," said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the right-leaning American Action Forum and a former director of the Congressional Budget Office. "It's not numerically reasonable."

The rapid recent increase in Treasury yields has added to angst over long-term US debt sustainability. Bessent's self-identified benchmark, the 10-year rate, exceeded 5% on Monday. That's a level it's rarely traded at since the early 2000s. Bessent may face questions over his strategy at a House Financial Services Committee hearing Tuesday morning.

While Bessent predicts the artificial intelligence boom will help US growth accelerate, the consensus view is 3% gross domestic product rises aren't in the offing soon. Both the median forecast of economists surveyed by Bloomberg and the International Monetary Fund's latest projections show little more than 2% for 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Wyndee Parker: National security adviser, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)
articles.summary: No two days are the same for Wyndee Parker. As national security adviser to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Parker is responsible for overseeing the activities of all of the lower chamber’s national security committees, including Armed Services, Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, Homeland Security and their Appropriations counterparts. She also works with the executive branch…
articles.body:
No two days are the same for Wyndee Parker.

As national security adviser to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Parker is responsible for overseeing the activities of all of the lower chamber’s national security committees, including Armed Services, Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, Homeland Security and their Appropriations counterparts.

She also works with the executive branch and its corresponding agencies that make up the entire intelligence community, including the CIA, National Security Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department, State Department and some elements of the Department of Homeland Security.

Day to day, she helps ensure information is flowing to Congress and lawmakers and their staff are “kept as informed as they should be about all of the executive branch activities, operations, etc.,” often working with the National Security Council to ensure that the right briefings come together.

On top of that, Parker ensures Jeffries is prepared for “a lot” of meetings with foreign dignitaries and senior executive branch officials, and she helps work on and review legislation that moves out of committees and onto the House floor, such as the National Defense Authorization Act — one of the largest bills Congress passes annually.

Parker admits she was “a little skeptical” when she came to Capitol Hill 25 years ago to serve as counsel on the House Intelligence Committee. That was a few years after receiving her law degree from Ohio State University and working in the office of general counsels for both the CIA and FBI.

“My supervisor at the time told me ‘you know, no day is like any other day that’s gone before.’ … A couple decades later, I’m saying the same thing said to me,” she said, attributing it to the nature of national security work.

“The world is so dynamic. It keeps us definitely motivated and kind of energized,” Parker said before adding that the phone rings “too often, I should say, between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m.”

Prior to working for Jeffries, Parker was with another senior member of the Democratic Party for nearly 15 years: former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), also serving as her national security adviser.

When she’s not up to her neck in national security matters, Parker said she relishes spending time with her husband and two children.

articles.title: Carrie Hughes: Health and human services director, House Education and the Workforce Committee
articles.summary: Carrie Hughes knows she is somewhat of a rarity on Capitol Hill. Her first job as a congressional aide was in the office of Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.). Eighteen years later, he’s the only member she has worked for. Hughes started in Scott’s personal office and now serves as the director of Health and…
articles.body:
Carrie Hughes knows she is somewhat of a rarity on Capitol Hill.

Her first job as a congressional aide was in the office of Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.). Eighteen years later, he’s the only member she has worked for.

Hughes started in Scott’s personal office and now serves as the director of Health and Human Services for the House Education and the Workforce Committee, where Scott is the ranking member.

“I do know and remember and have lived through some fights that rear their heads again,” Hughes said.

Those fights may look slightly different, she added, “but having the historical knowledge and having been through it before, I think can be very helpful.”

Hughes said she takes pride in working for a committee that has a tangible impact on people’s lives on issues like job-based health insurance, school meals and family violence prevention.

“I just feel like a lot of our work is really kind of doing good things for people to make their lives better and easier, and that’s, I think, as rewarding as it can get,” Hughes said.

Still, Hughes lamented the broad changes in political dynamics over the years that have made it more difficult for lawmakers to want to form consensus.

“I think there are instances where issues could be bipartisan, and should be bipartisan, and historically have been bipartisan, but there’s just not as much interest in that because it’s not as expeditious or convenient,” Hughes said. “I think that there’s been a lot more of [the majority] is just rowing in the direction that [President] Trump says … and there’s not a lot of room for debate.”

As a veteran Democratic healthcare staffer, Hughes spent years fighting to preserve the Affordable Care Act (ACA), which limited how much else the committee could accomplish. The current focus on affordability finally gives an opportunity to move past the ACA battles.

“I think affordability is always going to be on people’s minds, but we definitely have a little bit more vocal interest in that area from our members,” Hughes said.

“We were just kind of in this cycle of protecting and then repealing, then protecting and repealing. Where I think we all are looking forward to are opportunities to really build on the progress we’ve made and make things better for workers.”

articles.title: The time Scott Bessent tried to outsmart the bond market
articles.summary: Scott Bessent joined the Trump administration last year armed with formidable experience in markets, the widespread respect of Wall Street and limitless conf...
articles.body:
Scott Bessent joined the Trump administration last year armed with formidable experience in markets, the widespread respect of Wall Street and limitless confidence.

Bessent has brought to his role as Treasury secretary and President Donald Trump's point man on the economy the same swagger that famously allowed him to help George Soros "break" the Bank of England in 1992 by betting bet heavily against the pound. The trade forced the UK to abandon its efforts to prop up the currency – and netted Soros more than a billion dollars.

Bessent has recently dared traders to cross him by boldly declaring, "I am the house now." He's dismissed criticism by saying if "some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I'm doing, well, that's too bad." And he's promised to ease the cost of money by driving down bond yields.

But his efforts to outsmart the bond market – the deepest and most important market on the planet – have not lived up to the hype. If anything, critics say his efforts have backfired.

"The data is clear. He's added accelerant to the fire. He's had the exact opposite impact that he wanted," said Tim Mahedy, CEO of Access/Macro and a former official at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and the International Monetary Fund.

Early last year, Bessent said he wanted to lower the all-important 10-year yield below 4%. Instead, the opposite has happened, with the benchmark rate briefly climbing above 5.04% on Tuesday for the first time since 2007.

With rates rising uncomfortably high last month, Bessent surprised many on Wall Street with a controversial intervention that ultimately tripled Treasury buybacks.

But the plan has not been effective. Bond yields are higher now than before Bessent intervened, an increase that will make it more expensive for consumers to get a mortgage, mom-and-pop shops to get a small business loan and for Washington to borrow.

"It massively flopped," Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat, an investment research firm, told CNN earlier this month. "If anything, this may have made the problem worse. Bessent showed his hand. To investors, it was like, 'Oh my gosh, he's worried.' We should be too."

The Bessent move drew criticism from his mentor, legendary investor Stanley Druckenmiller, who penned an ( AI-assisted ) op-ed in The Wall Street Journal warning that efforts to suppress yields would backfire.

Douglas Holtz-Eakin, a top economist under President George W. Bush, said Bessent's move to control yields was "doomed to fail" because it didn't address the elephant in the room: Trillion-dollar deficits as far as the eye can see.

articles.title: Moody's Mark Zandi warns of a 'serious' mistake if the Fed hikes rates as Wall Street expects a quarter-point increase
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, but Zandi says higher rates won’t fix inflation.
articles.body:
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi is prodding the Federal Reserve to hold off on raising interest rates as most Fed watchers expect it to in the coming days.

The Fed is scheduled to have its next meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday, with Kevin Warsh over three months into the job as Fed chair. So far, Warsh has focused on scaling back economic guidance from the central bank to financial markets in a move that investors greeted with some unease on Wall Street. He's also set out to remake how Fed policymakers reach their interest rate decisions.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Warsh, though, has maintained he will endorse raising borrowing costs if inflation doesn't cool anytime soon, thanks in large part to the price spikes connected to the Iran War that began in February. The bulk of Wall Street analysts believe the Fed will begin hiking rates for the first time since 2023. Zandi, though, is arguing the central bank should tread carefully.

"The odds of a serious Fed policy mistake are uncomfortably high and rising. Markets are all but certain the Fed will raise rates a quarter point at next week's meeting, and are pricing in more to come," Zandi said in an X post. He argues the US economy is still in good shape, citing steady 2% growth and relatively low unemployment as factors for central bank policymakers to consider when making rate hike decisions.

"Inflation is too high, to be sure, running above 3%," Zandi said . "But much of that is the fallout from higher energy prices and tariffs, supply shocks that rate hikes can't fix and that should fade on their own so long as inflation expectations stay anchored, as they have."

Zandi presented the economic landscape as a tricky one for the Fed to maneuver. The explosion in AI spending among tech giants has propped up equities and fueled demand for critical memory chips and other AI-related equipment to power the buildout. The latter has compounded inflation for certain products like smartphones, laptops and gaming consoles, in addition to the tariffs that President Donald Trump unilaterally implemented last year.

"To hit its inflation objective, the Fed either needs to rein in the AI boom or put even more pressure on the rest of the economy," he said. "Neither is a good outcome. Of course, it doesn't have to choose either. It can wait."

articles.title: Canada prioritises tax rulings for C$1bn-plus investments
articles.summary: The initiative comes as the country hosts the Canada Investment Summit and aims to provide additional support for global investors.
articles.body:
The Government of Canada will give priority to income tax ruling requests connected to investments of C$1bn ($719m) or more in the country.

In a statement, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) said the measure, which is effective immediately, is intended to give large investors the "clarity and certainty" they need to advance with their planned investments.

The measure was announced by Finance and National Revenue Minister François-Philippe Champagne.

Through the Advance Income Tax Rulings (AITR) programme, investors can seek a binding CRA decision on the application of Canadian income tax law to a proposed transaction before committing capital.

Champagne said: "When investors are considering major projects, certainty matters. By prioritising advance tax rulings for investments of C$1bn or more, we are giving them the clarity and predictability they need to invest with confidence, create opportunities and help build Canada's economic future."

The initiative comes as the country hosts the Canada Investment Summit and aims to provide additional support for some of the largest global investors.

It also follows a measure set out in the 2026 Spring Economic Update, which prioritised ruling requests linked to large-scale projects and other investments aligned with Canada's economic priorities.

These include investments aimed at improving productivity and supporting the clean economy.

Meanwhile, the CRA will continue to provide the established 90-business day service standard for other rulings requests that do not qualify for prioritised rulings.

According to CRA data, in the fiscal year that ended on 31 March 2025, 91% of rulings were ​issued within ⁠that 90-business day standard.

"Canada prioritises tax rulings for C$1bn-plus investments" was originally created and published by The Accountant , a GlobalData owned brand.
